questions.question: How did Jim feel when he woke up? Was everything okay for him?
questions.explanation: This question checks if children notice Jim’s grumpy feelings at the start, helping them identify feelings in themselves and others.

questions.question: Why do Jim’s friends tell him to stand up straight or smile? Did this make Jim feel better inside?
questions.explanation: This question helps children see that changing how you look outside doesn’t always change how you feel inside.

questions.question: What did Jim say or do when everyone kept asking him to do things to feel better?
questions.explanation: This helps kids follow the story events and notice how Jim’s mood does not instantly improve by others’ ideas.

questions.question: Have you ever felt grumpy, like Jim? What happened? What did you want to do?
questions.explanation: This connects the story to the children's own experiences, showing it’s normal to feel grumpy sometimes.

questions.question: Is it okay to feel grumpy, or do we always have to be happy? Why?
questions.explanation: This helps children accept that all feelings, including grumpiness, are a part of life and don’t need to be hidden.

questions.question: What did Jim do that showed he was sorry after he shouted at his friends?
questions.explanation: This question helps children recognize how we can feel sorry and make up with others after we feel upset.

questions.question: When Jim met Norman at the end, what did they do that helped Jim feel better?
questions.explanation: This shows children the power of having someone with you, even if you still feel grumpy, and that friends help just by being there.

questions.question: What can you do when you feel grumpy? Who can you talk to?
questions.explanation: Encourages children to think about ways to handle their own grumpy feelings and identify people they trust.

questions.question: If a friend is feeling grumpy, what could you do to help them? Would you make them do something, or just be with them?
questions.explanation: Helps children understand empathy, and that sometimes friends need company, not fixing, when they are sad.

moral: It's okay to feel grumpy sometimes, and you don't always have to pretend you feel happy. Talking about your feelings or just having a friend with you can help you feel better.
learning_objectives: Children will identify and name feelings, especially grumpiness.
Children will understand that it is normal and okay to feel all kinds of emotions.
Children will recognize that pretending to be happy does not always make grumpy feelings disappear.
Children will learn how to support themselves and friends when feeling grumpy or sad.
discussion_points: Why do you think Jim wanted to say he wasn’t grumpy even when he felt that way inside?
How can we tell when someone feels grumpy or sad, even if they are smiling?
Can you think of a time when you wanted to just sit with someone when you felt upset?
What are some kind things we can do when a friend is feeling grumpy?
Are there times when it is helpful to talk about your feelings with someone you trust?
